chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak from Abdullah ibn Jabala from Sama'ah from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'If a man has children, is it permissible for him to give his wealth to his relatives?' He said, 'It is his wealth; he does with it what he wishes until death comes to him. Indeed, the owner of the wealth may do with his wealth whatever he wishes as long as he is alive. If he wishes, he may gift it; if he wishes, he may give it in charity; and if he wishes, he may leave it until death comes to him. If he bequeaths it, then it is not more than one-third, except that the excellence lies in not neglecting those he supports and not harming his heirs.'
ai.seo_question: What is the limit of bequest in Shia Islam and can a person give their wealth to relatives instead of heirs?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Istibsar, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes the principle of absolute financial autonomy for a living person, distinguishing between the unrestricted right to dispose of wealth during one's lifetime and the specific constraints of bequest (wasiyyah) upon death. He clarifies that while a bequest is limited to one-third of the estate, it is highly preferable (fadl) to ensure dependents are not neglected and heirs are not unduly harmed, reflecting the Shia emphasis on balancing individual rights with familial welfare. This ruling underscores the flexibility in Islamic inheritance law, allowing for charitable or relative-focused distribution before the mandatory shares take effect.
